To find the sharp upper bound on the diameter of $G$ as a function of $t$, consider the condition that the maximal homogeneous ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ is an associated prime of the $t$-th power of the closed neighborhood ideal $NI(G)^t$. 

This implies there exists a monomial $M$ such that $(NI(G)^t : M) = \mathfrak{m}$. Thus, for each vertex $x \in V(G)$, we have $xM \in NI(G)^t$ while $M \notin NI(G)^t$. Consequently, for any vertex $x$, $xM$ must be divisible by a generator $m_{w_1} \dots m_{w_t} \in NI(G)^t$, where each $m_{w_i} = \prod_{u \in N[w_i]} x_u$ corresponds to the closed neighborhood of a vertex $w_i$. Because $M \notin NI(G)^t$, $x$ must lie in the closed neighborhood of at least one of these centers $w_i$, meaning $\operatorname{dist}(x, w_i) \le 1$.

Each generator $m_{w_i}$ has support $N[w_i]$, which is a closed ball of radius $1$ (and thus diameter at most $2$) in the graph metric. Along any shortest path $P$, the intersection $N[w_i] \cap V(P)$ spans a subpath of length at most $2$. Therefore, a collection of $t$ such closed neighborhoods can cover a path of length at most $2 \times t = 2t$. By the triangle inequality and the connectedness constraints imposed by $\mathfrak{m} \in \operatorname{Ass}(NI(G)^t)$, the maximum possible distance between any two vertices in $G$ cannot exceed $2t$, and this bound is sharp.

ANSWER: 2t
